items.title: FOI lawsuits on origins of Covid-19,  gain-of-function research and biolabs
items.summary: U.S. Right to Know, a nonprofit newsroom and public health research group, has filed 46 lawsuits against federal and state agencies for violating Freedom of Information laws. The lawsuits are part of our efforts to uncover what is known about the origins of novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, leaks or mishaps at biosafety labs, and the risks of gain-of-function research that seeks to augment the infectivity or lethality of potential pandemic pathogens. We have filed 298 state, federal, and international public records requests seeking information about the origins of SARS-CoV-2, and the risks of biosafety labs and gain-of-function research. Read more about our findings so far , why we are conducting this investigation , recommended readings and documents we have obtained in our investigations. FOI lawsuits filed (46) U.S. Department of State : On August 18, 2026, USRTK filed a lawsuit against the State Department for violating provisions of the FOIA. The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, seeks cable traffic between the State Department and the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT Taipei) that relates to Taiwanese data or assessments about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic. Case 3:26-cv-08558. (45) Department of Energy: On April 28, 2026, USRTK filed a lawsuit against the DOE for violating provisions of the FOIA. items.title: CIA Release Reveals Internal Bin Laden Raid Talking Points, Q&A and Declassification Records
items.summary: A newly obtained Central Intelligence Agency release provides a detailed look at the material prepared inside the U.S. government for the public rollout following the May 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden, including internal talking points, an extensive question-and-answer package, public-affairs guidance and records documenting the expedited declassification of intelligence imagery. The 35-page responsive record was provided by the CIA in response to a Freedom of Information Act request filed by The Black Vault with the agency in August 2013. In its July 6, 2026, final response, the CIA said it had located the document in its “database of previously-released records” after determining that an earlier FOIA request had sought records on the same subject. Searches conducted for this article, however, did not locate the complete document in the CIA’s online Electronic Reading Room or elsewhere through conventional web searches. Some portions may therefore be newly accessible online through this release, although that cannot be fully established. What can be established is that this newly obtained package brings together internal records showing how that information was prepared, cleared and organized for public disclosure. items.title: New CIA Release Reveals More About Counterterrorism Problems Before 9/11
items.summary: A new CIA release obtained by The Black Vault has restored significant portions of an August 2001 Inspector General review of the agency’s Counterterrorist Center, adding details that had remained classified when the report was publicly released more than 15 years ago. The document, titled Inspection Report of the DCI Counterterrorist Center, Directorate of Operations , was completed in August 2001. An earlier version was approved for release to the public on July 26, 2010. The Black Vault requested a new Mandatory Declassification Review of the report on January 8, 2019. In a July 6, 2026 final response, the CIA said it had completed that re-review and “determined that additional information can be released.” The agency said remaining deletions were being maintained under Executive Order 13526 and statutory protections incorporated through FOIA Exemption (b)(3). A comparison of the two versions confirms that the new release does contain additional information. Much of it consists of statistics, organizational details and fuller passages that were only partially visible, or completely removed, in the 2010 copy. Numerous operational details, program names, personnel figures and other information remain classified. New Details on the Center’s Growth One of the clearest additions appears in the report’s executive summary. The 2010 version stated that Counterterrorist Center resources had increased over five years, but the actual personnel and budget figures were removed. It…

items.title: Navy Releases Hundreds of Pages on Cold War-Era “Advanced Naval Vehicles,” Including Nuclear-Powered Aircraft and High-Speed Warship Concepts
items.summary: A newly completed Freedom of Information Act release from the U.S. Navy provides hundreds of pages of detailed technical, cost and mission analysis from a late-1970s effort to determine what the next generation of naval vehicles might look like, which includes nuclear-powered aircraft designed to remain on station for days, 80-knot surface-effect ships, enormous lighter-than-air vehicles, wing-in-ground-effect craft and unconventional high-speed warships. The records concern the Advanced Naval Vehicles Concepts Evaluation, or ANVCE, Project, a Navy study begun in 1975 to help shape research and development for the 1980–2000 period. The project ultimately examined nine broad vehicle concepts through more than 200 studies, tests and experiments. Volume 1 states that candidate vehicles were judged against three basic requirements: they had to “be technically feasible,” “have military value,” and “be affordable.” The Navy released the records September 23, 2026, in response to a FOIA request filed by The Black Vault in September 2023. According to the response, the Navy located Volumes 1, 2 and 3, along with the appendices to Volume 4, consisting of 939 pages in all. The Navy said the Volume 3 appendices and the main Volume 4 report were still being digitized for later review and release, meaning the current production is not yet the complete ANVCE collection. Portions remain withheld under FOIA Exemption (b)(1) , covering information the Navy says remains properly classified…

items.title: FBI Files on Cryptography – FBI File #80-HQ-612
items.summary: Background Before the modern era, cryptography was concerned solely with message confidentiality (i.e., encryption)—conversion of messages from a comprehensible form into an incomprehensible one and back again at the other end, rendering it unreadable by interceptors or eavesdroppers without secret knowledge (namely the key needed for decryption of that message). Encryption attempted to ensure secrecy in communications, such as those of spies, military leaders, and diplomats. In recent decades, the field has expanded beyond confidentiality concerns to include techniques for message integrity checking, sender/receiver identity authentication, digital signatures, interactive proofs and secure computation, among others. Below, you will find the declassified FBI File that was labeled “Cryptography.” The file stretches back to the mid to late 1930s! It is an ongoing FOIA request, wherein many documents have not been released yet, and are being reviewed by multiple agencies. I will continue to add the releases, as they become available. Suspected Military Retrieval and Witness Accounts Project Blue Book Files: The Official Investigation NASA’s Involvement and the Missing “Fragology” Files New Findings via The Black Vault (2021 FOIA Releases) Conclusion Executive Summary The Kecksburg UFO incident of December 9, 1965 remains one of the most intriguing unresolved cases of a mysterious object falling from the sky. Often dubbed “Pennsylvania’s Roswell,” it involved reports of a fiery fireball streaking over several U.S. states and Canada, a crash in the woods near the village of Kecksburg, and an alleged military recovery of an unknown object [1] . Over the decades, the incident has been the subject of intense speculation – from meteor to secret Cold War satellite to extraterrestrial craft – and persistent efforts by investigators to unearth official records. This deep dive examines all angles of the Kecksburg case, drawing on eyewitness accounts, media reports, and released government documents (many obtained via The Black Vault’s FOIA requests) to present a balanced, evidence-backed picture of what we know. items.title: The Pangram Paradox: The Problem with AI “Detecting” other AIs
items.summary: Op-ed: This is an opinion piece published on Unlimited Hangout . Most articles published on UH are not opinion pieces, so we are clearly labeling those that are. It should be no secret to readers of Unlimited Hangout that I have a very negative view of the impact that Artificial Intelligence (AI) is having on independent media and media in general. As someone who has been impersonated by AI daily on large video platforms for a few years now, I have come to acutely feel that AI is becoming a dangerous force that is making it increasingly difficult for well-meaning readers/viewers to distinguish between what is real and what is false. I don’t mean just for those hoping to view my content, as the personal issue I am facing is a microcosm of a much larger problem. As a result, one might think that I would have been pleased, if not relieved, to see Substack, a large platform for professional writers, partner with an “AI detection tool.” Not only am I not pleased, but I have now taken the time to write an opinion piece explaining why I think this is bad and to also explain where I think a lot of this is going. Substack’s new partner and, apparently, the AI detection tool of choice for most major media outlets right now is called Pangram. Pangram was founded in 2023, originally under the name Checkfor.ai, by Max Spero and Bradley Emi.
